==Problem==

How many rearrangements of <imath>abcd</imath> are there in which no two adjacent letters are also adjacent letters in the alphabet?  For example, no such rearrangements could include either <imath>ab</imath> or <imath>ba</imath>.

<imath> \textbf{(A)}\ 0\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 1\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 2\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 3\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 4</imath>

==Solution 1==
The first thing one would want to do is place a possible letter that works and then stem off of it.  For example, if we start with an <imath>a</imath>, we can only place a <imath>c</imath> or <imath>d</imath> next to it.  Unfortunately, after that step, we can't do too much, since:

<imath>acbd</imath> is not allowed because of the <imath>cb</imath>, and <imath>acdb</imath> is not allowed because of the <imath>cd</imath>. 

We get the same problem if we start with a <imath>d</imath>, since a <imath>b</imath> will have to end up in the middle, causing it to be adjacent to an <imath>a</imath> or <imath>c</imath>.

If we start with a <imath>b</imath>, the next letter would have to be a <imath>d</imath>, and since we can put an <imath>a</imath> next to it and then a <imath>c</imath> after that, this configuration works.  The same approach applies if we start with a <imath>c</imath>.

So the solution must be the two solutions that were allowed, one starting from a <imath>b</imath> and the other with a <imath>c</imath>, giving us:

<cmath>1 + 1 = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 2}.</cmath>


==Solution 2 (Casework)==

'''Case 1: the first letter is A'''

''Subcase 1: the second letter is C''

The next letter must either be B or D, both of which do not satisfy the conditions.

''Subcase 2: the second letter is D''

The third letter is forced to be B and the fourth is forced to be C, but this doesn't work because B and C are next to each other.

'''Case 2: the first letter is B'''

The next letter is forced to be D, the third letter forced to be A and the last forced to be C. This works.

'''Case 3: the first letter is C'''

The next letter is forced to be A, the third letter is D and the last letter is B. This works.

'''Case 4: the first letter is D'''

''Subcase 1: the second letter is A''

The third letter has to be C and the fourth has to be B but this doesn't work because B and C are next to each other.

''Subcase 2: the second letter is B''

The third letter cannot be A or C, so this doesn't work.

Summing the cases, there are two that work: <imath>BDAC</imath> and <imath>CADB</imath> <imath>\Longrightarrow \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 2}</imath>.

~JH. L


==Solution 3==

We note that <imath>a</imath> must be adjacent to <imath>c</imath> or <imath>d</imath>, <imath>b</imath> must be adjacent to <imath>d</imath>, <imath>c</imath> must be adjacent to <imath>a</imath>, and <imath>d</imath> must be adjacent to <imath>a</imath> or <imath>b</imath>. In other words, the way the letters can be connected is <cmath>c-a-d-b.</cmath> Therefore, the only two possible arrangements are <imath>cadb</imath> and <imath>bdac</imath>, which gives <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 2}</imath>.


==Solution 4==
Notice that <imath>b</imath> and <imath>c</imath> cannot be in the middle because they would be forced to be next to at least one letter that is next to them in the alphabet(For example, if <imath>b</imath> was in the middle the only letter that can be next to <imath>b</imath> is <imath>d</imath> but since it's in the middle it needs another letter, which means that it's not possible). Therefore you either have a case starting with <imath>b</imath>(then it has to be followed by <imath>d</imath> then <imath>a</imath> then <imath>c</imath>) or starting with <imath>c</imath>, amounting to <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 2}</imath> cases
